newsitem.title: UK: SIB was concerned about driving business off LME.
newsitem.headline: SIB was concerned about driving business off LME.

text.p: British regulator the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) opted to tighten rules on practices peculiar to the London Metal Exchange (LME), but was wary of driving customers away from the market.

"It would damage the price formation process and the market as a whole if you introduced so much unnecessary red tape into regulation that legitmate business went offshore and off exchange," SIB chairman Andrew Large told Reuters.
The review of the LME after a six-month consultation exercise found that non-cash clearing and other practices such as historic price carries did not in principle threaten the financial system.
In non-cash clearing, also referred to as collateralised clearing, positions only become payable when the due date becomes prompt.

"There is no reason why collateralised clearing should lead to increased levels of systemic risk, since all LME exchange contracts registered with the LCH (London Clearing House) for clearing are marked to market daily and any resulting loss in the value of the positions is fully collateralised," the SIB report said.

The report said a majority of the 94 respondents to an SIB questionnaire were strongly in favour of continuing non-cash clearing since it matched the cash flow of their hedges to the cash flows arising from transactions in physical metal.
Regarding historic price carries (HPCs), the SIB said the practice could continue, but more controls were needed.
A minority of LME users responding to the questionnaire said they used the facility, in which customers may roll forward expiring positions at the original price, and urged the SIB not to scrap it.
Rival exchange NYMEX, which also trades copper, told the SIB in its response the practice was unwise, allowing customers to effectively mask the impact of any losses.

The SIB said in its review, "There is no doubt HPCs should be used by customers only with an appropriate control environment...and we therefore recommend a tightening of the LME's rules in relation to this facility."
However, added regulation might be costly, SIB officials said.
"It may be that, after consideration of the costs and benefits, the LME, as a commercial decision, may elect to withdraw the facility," the SIB report said.
The SIB also allowed LME ring members to continue to advance credit to customers to meet margin obligations and to mix customers' funds with their own funds.

The current practice, in which customers are allowed to decide whether they want their own funds segregated, however, increased risk to customers, and regulators would make sure these risks were made known to customers, the SIB review said.
LME users told the SIB they were aware of the risks and agreed to the practice in exchange for credit facilities and reduced charges from LME members.
